item.title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
item.dc:creator: Erjian Cheng
Yixing Yang
Yifan Gao
Jan Priessnitz
Yiqing Hao
Jieyi Liu
Rui Lou
Alexander Fedorov
item.description:
Authors: Erjian Cheng, Yixing Yang, Yifan Gao, Jan Priessnitz, Yiqing Hao, Jieyi Liu, Rui Lou, Alexander Fedorov, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p -wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs. 1–3 ). Achieving p -wave superconductivity 4 and its magnetic analogue 5 —characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric, p -wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge 6,7 . Despite recent progress in identifying candidate p -wave magnets 5,7–10 , spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for p -wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal p -wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves S y polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted S y exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p -wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p -wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics 10 , topological matter 7 , superconductivity 11 and beyond.

item.title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
item.dc:creator: Z. Wang
C. Moulsdale
X. Guo
J. Liu
Z. Qiu
I. Soltero
Z. Jiang
M. Holwill
item.description:
Authors: Z. Wang, C. Moulsdale, X. Guo, J. Liu, Z. Qiu, I. Soltero, Z. Jiang, M. Holwill, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies 1–4 . Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases 2,5,6 . However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space 7–12 ), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.

item.title: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
item.dc:creator: Simon Wili
Meng-Zi Huang
Tommaso Bonaccorsi
Michael U. Mühlematter
Mohsen Talebi
Yaakov Yudkin
Alex Gómez-Salvador
Filip Marijanovic
item.description:
Authors: Simon Wili, Meng-Zi Huang, Tommaso Bonaccorsi, Michael U. Mühlematter, Mohsen Talebi, Yaakov Yudkin, Alex Gómez-Salvador, Filip Marijanovic, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections 1–3 , and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips 4 . In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model 5 . The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

item.title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
item.dc:creator: Hui Chen
Linnea Rosberg
David Dreyer
Bo Leberecht
Henrik Mouritsen
Pauline N. Fleischmann
Eric J. Warrant
item.description:
Authors: Hui Chen, Linnea Rosberg, David Dreyer, Bo Leberecht, Henrik Mouritsen, Pauline N. Fleischmann, Eric J. Warrant
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Bogong moths ( Agrotis infusa ) migrate biannually up to 1,000 km between their breeding areas and geographically restricted aestivation sites in the Australian Alps 1,2 . These moths navigate towards their distant goal using the stars as a compass 3 but navigate correctly even when the stars are obscured by clouds 3 , suggesting that their magnetic sense 4 probably harnesses the Earth’s magnetic field as a compass. However, the nature of this compass, and of the magnetic sense underlying it, remains unknown. Here we show that Bogong moths, tethered in a flight arena under a full-spectrum randomized starry night sky, navigate in their inherited migratory direction using the geomagnetic field alone. If the geomagnetic field is turned by 180°, or if inclination is inverted, moths fly in the opposite direction. If polarity is inverted, moths fail to turn. Furthermore, if violet–blue light (380 nm < λ < 500 nm) is removed from the illumination spectrum, or if tethered moths are exposed to weak broadband radiofrequency fields (150 kHz to 60 MHz), magnetic orientation is abolished. Our results indicate that Bogong moths use the geomagnetic field as an inclination compass for long-distance navigation at night and possess a light-dependent radical-pair-based magnetic sense 5 .

item.title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape
item.dc:creator: Lukas Ramsauer
Anna-Marie Pedde
Anna Hirschberger
María Parra Reyes
Nadine Nuschele
Felix Bayerl
Sebastian Lacher
Sainitin Donakonda
item.description:
Authors: Lukas Ramsauer, Anna-Marie Pedde, Anna Hirschberger, María Parra Reyes, Nadine Nuschele, Felix Bayerl, Sebastian Lacher, Sainitin Donakonda, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies 1–7 . Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers 1–4,8,9 . Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8 + T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies 10–13 . However, ferroptotic cells limit this response 8–10,14 , resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2 ), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8 + T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca 2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE 2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE 2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE 2 production or disrupting PGE 2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8 + T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

item.title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
item.dc:creator: Morgan Gaïa
Ulysse Guyet
Hans-Joachim Ruscheweyh
A. Murat Eren
Shinichi Sunagawa
Eugene V. Koonin
Mart Krupovic
Tom O. Delmont
item.description:
Authors: Morgan Gaïa, Ulysse Guyet, Hans-Joachim Ruscheweyh, A. Murat Eren, Shinichi Sunagawa, Eugene V. Koonin, Mart Krupovic, Tom O. Delmont
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution 1–4 . They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals 5,6 . Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes 7 , and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology 8 . Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of Trichomonas vaginalis 9 and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

item.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
item.dc:creator: Weikang Han
Tingting Lu
Wenkun Xie
Jinxi Yuan
Chengwei Lu
Lei Shang
Guirong Wang
Bill S. Hansson
item.description:
Authors: Weikang Han, Tingting Lu, Wenkun Xie, Jinxi Yuan, Chengwei Lu, Lei Shang, Guirong Wang, Bill S. Hansson, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics 1,2 . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented 2 , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria , guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei . Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

item.title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
item.dc:creator: Yansheng Zhang
Feiyang Wang
Paul H. C. Wong
Alexander C. Jenkins
Yi Jiang
Konstantinos Konstantinou
Gehrig Carlse
Nishant Dogra
item.description:
Authors: Yansheng Zhang, Feiyang Wang, Paul H. C. Wong, Alexander C. Jenkins, Yi Jiang, Konstantinos Konstantinou, Gehrig Carlse, Nishant Dogra, et al.
Journal: Nature; Volume: 659; Issue: 8141; Pages: 634-639
Abstract: Abstract Quantum field theories provide fundamental models of complex interacting systems 1–3 , from high-energy physics and cosmology to condensed matter. However, solving these models in non-perturbative and dynamical regimes is often challenging, particularly in more than one spatial dimension. Analogue simulation using tunable synthetic quantum systems can both verify existing theoretical predictions and lead to physical insights. Here we realize analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time), using two coherently coupled spin components 4,5 in a uniform two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate 6,7 . Specifically, we encode the paradigmatic sine-Gordon model 8,9 in the long-wavelength modes of the field describing the relative phase, ϕ , of the two components. In the perturbative regime, collective field excitations exhibit a relativistic dispersion with a tunable mass gap. We also observe explicitly non-perturbative phenomena, including the existence of topological domain walls across which ϕ rapidly winds by 2π (ref. 10 ). Our work opens possibilities for studies of cosmologically relevant phenomena including preheating 11,12 , dynamics of topological defects 13,14 and relativistic false-vacuum decay 15–19 .

item.title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
item.dc:creator: Antonio Fieramosca
Vincenzo Ardizzone
Rosanna Mastria
Eugenio Maggiolini
Laura Polimeno
Umberto Dellasette
Andrea Notargiacomo
Marialilia Pea
item.description:
Authors: Antonio Fieramosca, Vincenzo Ardizzone, Rosanna Mastria, Eugenio Maggiolini, Laura Polimeno, Umberto Dellasette, Andrea Notargiacomo, Marialilia Pea, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing 1 . Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses 2 . Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms 3–5 . However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

item.title: Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum
item.dc:creator: Jia-Wu Feng
Congcong Jiang
Beáta Strejčková
Marek Szecówka
Einar Baldvin Haraldsson
Thomas Lux
Chaodan An
Micha Bayer
item.description:
Authors: Jia-Wu Feng, Congcong Jiang, Beáta Strejčková, Marek Szecówka, Einar Baldvin Haraldsson, Thomas Lux, Chaodan An, Micha Bayer, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract The genus Hordeum comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses 1,2 . Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during Hordeum diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into Hordeum , with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes Hordeum as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering new avenues for barley improvement.

item.title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
item.dc:creator: Nathaly R. Guerrero-Ramírez
Jan Salecker
Craig E. Simpkins
Fabian Brambach
Marife D. Corre
Kevin F. A. Darras
Jochen Drescher
Ingo Grass
item.description:
Authors: Nathaly R. Guerrero-Ramírez, Jan Salecker, Craig E. Simpkins, Fabian Brambach, Marife D. Corre, Kevin F. A. Darras, Jochen Drescher, Ingo Grass, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity 1 in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices 2–4 . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.
